newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Maori make presence felt in new N.Zealand cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Maori make presence felt in new N.Zealand cabinet.

text.p: Three Maori ministers were chosen by Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Sunday in his cabinet for the newly formed National-New Zealand First coalition that he said would govern with greater fairness and compassion.
"The ministry is a bold reflection of the diversity in New Zealand," Bolger told a news conference.
"The range of experience, age and ideas makes this the most representative executive in New Zealand's history."

Bolger said the new cabinet, in which three former ministers were dumped to make room for five New Zealand First cabinet slots, was a response to the demands of the country's new proportional representation system of government.
The three Maori cabinet members are all from New Zealand First which is dominated by Maori members of parliament, including its leader and Deputy Prime Minister, Winston Peters.
Under the appointments, Peters becomes treasurer, John Delamere becomes associate treasurer and Tau Henare receives Maori affairs.
But of the 20-member cabinet, only one -- State Services and State-Owned Enterprises Minister Jenny Shipley -- is a woman, something Bolger was apologetic for.
"It's true we are light on women," he said.

The Polynesian Maori population, comprising 13 percent of the nation's total, is under-represented in positions of power but greatly over-repesented in statistics for crime, poor education and training and health problems.

NZ First held the balance of power with 17 of 120 members of parliament and last week dramatically chose to side with the conservative and ruling National Party over left-leaning Labour after an eight weeks of talks.

Three of six ministers outside of the cabinet are women, including 26-year-old Youth Affairs Minister Deborah Morris, and Bolger promised to promote some of them in a cabinet review scheduled for 1998.
The decision to share power with New Zealand First was largely responsible for the softening of the conservative National Party's six years of monetarist rule from 1990.
Peters grabbed for himself the powerful role of treasurer but he also secured seven other ministerial posts for his party colleagues, disproportionate to the party's 13 percent of the vote.
Key areas where Peters and his party are likely to soften policy include education and health, where attempts to run public hospitals on a profit basis have largely been abandoned.
Bill English takes over from the hardline Shipley as health minister and he will spend more and attempt to get health issues off the front pages of newspapers.

Regional health boards will be abandoned and the ministry will get a NZ$1.7 billion (US$1.2 billion) transfusion over three years. In education, an extra NZ$824 million is to be spent over the next three years.
Peters believes much Maori underachievement is the result of many getting a slow start at school.
But not all planned reforms soften National's hard edges.

People on unemployment benefits will be required to train or work for "the dole". And prisoners are going to have to work from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., a move civil libertarians suggest might breach human rights. ($1 = NZ$1.43)
